title: Reading a pauri of Bhai Gurdas
hook: a slow reading of one pauri, its picture, its point

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rehat Maryada, and your line, the two voices allowed. Which line did you decide to keep on purpose? Day seven hundred nineteen.

A forest. Tall trees, thick undergrowth, a bamboo grove rattling in the wind. And somewhere in the middle, one sandalwood tree. That's the whole opening of the stanza we're reading today. No hero, no journey, no miracle. Just trees standing next to each other. For days now we've heard about Bhai Gurdas and his vars. Today we stop talking about him and read him slowly, the way a ragi or a katha teacher would. Today: pauri.
screen: `A FOREST, A BAMBOO GROVE.` → `ONE SANDALWOOD TREE.` → `TODAY, WE READ HIM SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: A pauri is one stanza of a var, and Bhai Gurdas often builds his around a picture you could find in any village. So read in three steps. Step one: the picture. Let it stand before you look for meaning. A sandalwood tree grows in the forest, and its fragrance spreads. The trees around it, ordinary trees, pick up its scent. That's all. Stay with it. Step two: the twist. Bhai Gurdas pictures one tree that doesn't take the scent: the bamboo, standing right there beside the sandalwood. It's tall. It's hollow. Some readers hear pride in it: so taken up with its own height that the fragrance never gets in. Now the picture has tension. Closeness alone didn't change it. Step three: the point. For Bhai Gurdas, the sandalwood is the Guru, or the company of the Guru's Sikhs, the sangat. Ordinary people sitting near it take on something of its fragrance. But a person can sit right beside it, every week, and stay exactly the same, if they're hollow and puffed up with themselves. The pauri doesn't scold. It just shows you the bamboo and lets you notice it. That's the method. One picture, held long enough to see it. One twist that gives it an edge. One point, which the picture has already made before anyone states it.
screen: `STEP ONE: THE PICTURE.` · `STEP TWO: THE BAMBOO THAT STAYS THE SAME.` · `STEP THREE: THE POINT, THE SANGAT.` · `LET THE PICTURE MAKE THE POINT.` · then, large: `ONE PICTURE, ONE POINT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one pauri slowly. Today's will do. Close your eyes and build the picture first: the forest, the sandalwood, the ordinary trees around it slowly taking on its scent. Stay with the picture for the first part of the sit, without asking what it means. Then bring in the bamboo, tall and hollow, right beside it. Notice it. Only near the end, let the point arrive on its own. Where in your life are you sitting close to something good? If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly at the end. The bell holds the time.
Pauri, one stanza of a var, read first for its picture, then its twist, then the point that comes out of the picture itself.
Your line: one picture, one point. Today, when something strikes you, hold the picture before you decide what it means. Day seven hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: In katha, a teacher in the gurdwara takes one pauri of Bhai Gurdas, describes its picture, and draws out its point for the sangat, often alongside a line of Gurbani.

fork.setup: a sandalwood tree grows in the forest, and its scent spreads. which tree stays without the fragrance?
fork.reveal: in the pauri, it's the bamboo, right beside the sandalwood, hollow and tall, that never takes the scent.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty picture of trees.
what it means: the sangat changes people, but nearness alone isn't enough if you're hollow with pride.
what a scholar hears: the pauri's method: the picture makes the point before anyone states it.
